reason: There is a wealth of consistent information across multiple sources regarding the discovery date, the naming controversy, and the role of the Herschel siblings.
story: William Herschel was a German-born musician living in Bath, England, when he accidentally doubled the size of the known solar system. On March 13, 1781, using a homemade reflecting telescope, he spotted a faint object he initially mistook for a comet. It was actually the first planet discovered since antiquity. Seeking to honor his royal patron, King George III, Herschel named the new world 'Georgium Sidus,' or 'George’s Star.' While the King was pleased—granting Herschel a salary and the title of Court Astronomer—international scientists were not. French astronomers refused to name a planet after a British monarch, often calling it 'Herschel' instead. Eventually, the community settled on 'Uranus,' following the mythological theme of other planets. Despite the name change, Herschel’s royal favor endured; he even secured a government salary for his sister and assistant, Caroline, making her the first woman paid for scientific services in England.
angle: The discoverer of Uranus tried to name the planet 'George' to flatter the King of England, but international outrage forced a change to a Greek god instead.

claims.claim: William Herschel discovered Uranus on March 13, 1781.
Herschel initially mistook the planet for a comet.
Uranus was the first planet discovered since antiquity.
Uranus was the first planet ever discovered using a telescope.
Herschel was a professional musician and composer before becoming a famous astronomer.
The discovery was made from Herschel's back garden in Bath, England.
Herschel proposed the name 'Georgium Sidus' (George's Star) for the new planet.
The name was chosen to honor King George III of the United Kingdom.
International astronomers rejected the name because it did not follow the mythological pattern of other planets.
Johann Bode suggested the name 'Uranus' in 1782.
In France, the planet was often called 'Herschel' to avoid naming it after the British King.
Caroline Herschel served as William's constant assistant and observation recorder.
Caroline Herschel was the first woman in England to be granted a government salary for scientific work.
Herschel discovered the two largest moons of Uranus, Titania and Oberon.
The telescopes Herschel used featured mirrors made of speculum metal.
Herschel's homemade telescope for the discovery had a 6.2-inch aperture.
Herschel also discovered infrared radiation while testing filters for solar observation.
Uranus is twice as distant from the Sun as Saturn.

disputed: The specific title 34 Tauri is only mentioned by one source as the star Uranus was previously mistaken for; the script should refer to it generally as a 'fixed star' instead.
The exact number of comets discovered by Caroline is described as 8 by most sources, but one mentions she found 'seven other comets' after her first discovery, confirming the total.
